1:
The opening formula is a date, and what it dates from is the point. Gill reads it as following the whole Bathsheba episode — the sin, the repentance for it, the pardon of it, and the birth of Solomon as a token of reconciliation; and yet, he insists, after all this the divine threatenings must still take place. They had begun already in the death of the child begotten in adultery, and what the chapter records is the next of them. Ellicott cautions against attaching the formula too narrowly, since it applies to the narrative which follows as a whole rather than to the genealogical fact mentioned immediately after it. On his reckoning the events probably occurred soon after the Ammonite war and David's marriage with Bath-sheba.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the mechanism by which the threatened judgment arrives, and it is domestic rather than military. The judgments fell upon David and upon his house, but they were brought about by sins and crimes on the part of his own sons — for which, they argue, David was himself to blame twice over: partly through his own indulgence and want of discipline, and partly through the bad example he had set. The sons grew up without strict paternal discipline, simply under the care of their different mothers, who were jealous of one another; so they fancied they might gratify their own fleshly lusts and carry out their own ambitious plans. From this arose a series of crimes that nearly cost the king his life and throne.

Henry presses the same point as a warning rather than an analysis. Godly parents have often been afflicted with wicked children, since grace does not run in the blood though corruption does. He observes that David's children did not imitate him in his devotion, but his false steps they trod in, and in those did much worse, and repented not — and he draws the lesson for parents, that they know not how fatal the consequences may be if in any instance they give their children bad examples. Keil and Delitzsch map the shape of what follows: Amnon led the way with his violation of Tamar, the crime was avenged by her own brother Absalom, who assassinated Amnon, and Absalom was then obliged to flee to Geshur.

The relationships the crime turns on are set out carefully, because they are what make it what it is. Clarke identifies Tamar as the daughter of David and Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur, and so the uterine sister of Absalom; Amnon was David's eldest son by Ahinoam. The conclusion he draws is the hinge of the chapter — she was sister to Amnon only by the father's side, a half-sister, but whole sister to Absalom. Ellicott names the grandfather, Talmai king of Geshur, notes that Absalom at least had been born during David's reign at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:3), and confirms Amnon as David's first-born (2 Samuel 3:2). Henry adds the motive the verse itself supplies: she was fair, and therefore Amnon coveted her — beauty being a snare to many, as it was here to her.
2:
The verse reports a physical collapse, and Gill reads the vexation behind it as internal disorder — Amnon distressed, straitened and perplexed in his mind through the unruly and unbridled lusts that raged in him. Clarke reaches for Delaney to explain why this particular desire should waste a man's body, and the observation is that the passion of love is nowhere so wasting and vexatious as where it is unlawful. A quick sense of guilt, especially where the guilt is enormous, strikes the soul with horror; and the impossibility of an innocent gratification loads that horror with desperation, making a conflict too cruel and too dreadful for human bearing. On that reading the sickness is not incidental to the sin but produced by it.

What made the thing seem impossible is read off the household arrangements. Ellicott corrects the rendering — rather than thought it hard, the sense is that it seemed impossible to Amnon — and locates the obstacle in the modest seclusion of Tamar in the harem of her mother, which left him no opportunity to carry out his desires. He draws from the narrative the further fact that the king's children lived in different households, each grown-up son dwelling in his own house. Wesley makes the virginity itself the barrier: being a virgin she was diligently kept, so that he could not get private converse with her. Henry qualifies that precisely, holding that innocent converse with her was not denied him, and that what Amnon could not gain was an opportunity to solicit her chastity.

Henry then turns the sickness into the verse's own verdict on the appetite that caused it. Amnon was so vexed at being unable to find that opportunity that he fell sick, and the moral Henry draws is that fleshly lusts are their own punishment — they not only war against the soul but against the body too, and are the rottenness of the bones. From this he asks the reader to see what a hard master sinners serve, and how heavy his yoke is. Keil and Delitzsch note only what the condition made visible to others, that Amnon's miserable appearance was observed, which is what sets the next scene in motion.
3:
The man who solves Amnon's problem is introduced by his relation and his character. Gill notes the irony in the word friend, since in the issue his friendship proved Amnon's ruin. Henry sharpens it — so Amnon called him, but he was really an enemy to him — and describes a kinsman who had in him more of David's blood, being his nephew, than of David's spirit, a subtle man cunning to carry on any bad design. Ellicott is unwilling to let the word carry that weight on its own, holding that subtil indicates simply sagacity and wisdom, whether rightly or wrongly exercised. Clarke has no such reserve, calling the counsel that follows most diabolic advice.

The genealogy is worked out because the narrative gives it. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both note that Shimeah is called Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9, where he appears as the third son of Jesse; Ellicott adds that he had another son, Jonathan, named in 2 Samuel 21:21 as the conqueror of one of the giants. Clarke takes the episode as an argument against nostalgia, quoting the counsel not to ask what is the cause that the former days were better than these, and concluding that taken altogether we may thank God those times are past and pray that they may never return.

Jonadab's opening question is examined for what it assumes. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the wasting away precisely, the word meaning spare or shrunken and here equivalent to looking miserable, and explain the odd specification from morning to morning: the morning is mentioned because sick persons look worst then. Henry reads the appeal to Amnon's rank as a double temptation. Being the king's son, he has the pleasures of the court to divert him — on which Henry remarks that content and comfort are not always to be found in royal palaces, and asks with much more reason why dejected saints, who are children of the King of kings and heirs of the crown of life, should be thus lean from day to day.

The second half of the appeal Henry treats as the more dangerous. Being the king's son, Amnon has the power of a prince to command whatever he wants and wishes for, and need not pine for what, lawful or unlawful, he may have — your will is law. Henry sets beside it Jezebel's words to Ahab in a like case, Dost not thou govern Israel (1 Kings 21:7), and concludes that the abuse of power is the most dangerous temptation of the great. What Amnon returns is an admission: Henry notes that he had the impudence to own his wicked lust, miscalling it love.
5:
Gill describes the counsel as the work of a subtle man who at once formed a scheme to relieve Amnon and open a way for the enjoyment of what he desired. Henry measures it against what a friend would have done. Had Jonadab been what he pretended, he would have startled at the mention of such wickedness, laid before Amnon the evil of it, and used his subtlety to divert him — even by recommending some other person whom he might lawfully marry. Instead he shows no surprise at all, and objects neither to the unlawfulness nor to the difficulty, neither to the reproach nor so much as to his father's displeasure. Henry's verdict is general: the case of those is miserable whose friends, instead of admonishing and reproving them, flatter them and forward them in their sinful ways.

The feigned illness is carefully distinguished from the real one. Ellicott corrects the rendering to feign thyself sick, and points out that the sickness already reported was the genuine pining of ungoverned and ungratified passion, whereas this is a crafty imitation of it — though the first would lend colour and plausibility to the second. Henry works the same distinction from the other side: Amnon is already sick but still goes about, and must now take upon him to be so ill as to be unable to rise, his wasted looks supplying the credibility. The pretence extends to his appetite, so that dainty meat is abhorred (Job 33:20) and the best dish from the king's table cannot please him.

What he asks for is chosen for the access it gives rather than for the food. Keil and Delitzsch explain the dish itself, the verb being a denominative formed from the noun, and the cakes a heart-strengthening kind of pastry, something like a pancake, which could be very quickly made. Wesley reads both halves of the request as cover. In calling her my sister Amnon forestalls any suspicion of a dishonest design upon so near a relation, and in asking to eat at her hand he pretends a stomach so nice that he could take nothing but what he saw dressed, and that by a person whom he much esteemed. Ellicott notes the result such a request would naturally have: coming from an invalid it seemed reasonable, and was readily granted.

Both the father and the sister act from affection, and every witness marks it. Henry observes that David was always fond of his children and concerned if anything ailed them, so he comes himself to visit; but of the request he says plainly that David saw no reason to suspect any mischief, God having hid his heart from understanding in this matter, and that he gave the order innocently though he must afterwards have reflected on it with great regret. Ellicott notes where the order was sent — literally into the house, meaning the private apartments of the women. Gill supposes Tamar was perhaps not in the palace but at her brother Absalom's house, and says she went in obedience to the king's command and in affection to her brother, with an innocent breast, having no suspicion of any design upon her chastity. Henry adds that she neither dreaded abuse, having no cause to from a brother and a sick one, nor disdained the work: though a king's daughter, a great beauty and well dressed, she did not think it below her to knead cakes and bake them.
9:
The meal is finished and refused, and the refusal is read as part of the design. Gill describes the serving: she took a pan and poured the cakes out before him, out of the vessel they were cooked in and into another dish, the whole done in his presence so that he might see of what and in what manner it was made, and so that his stomach might not recoil at it. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the vessel itself, a word occurring only here, which the ancient versions take for a frying-pan or sauce-pan, though its etymology is uncertain; and they describe Amnon's response as that of a whimsical patient, refusing what he had asked for. Ellicott makes the same point about plausibility — the refusal seemed natural enough in an invalid of that temper.

Clearing the room is the step that matters, and it passes unchallenged for the same reason. Ellicott notes that the next requirement, have out all men from me, awakened no suspicion in the mind of Tamar. Henry supplies the motive the narrative withholds, that the adulterer is in care that no eye see him (Job 24:15): the meat is ready, but Amnon cannot eat while he is looked at by those about him, so they must all be turned out. The social convention did the rest, since the sick must be humoured and think they have a privilege to command. Wesley reconstructs the staging in two movements — Amnon lay on his couch in the chamber where the company were with him and where she had baked the cakes before him; he first sends them all out of that room, and then rises from the couch and, upon some pretence, goes into another and more private chamber.

The second removal is what isolates her. Gill describes the place as an inner chamber at a greater distance, where they might be more secret and out of the reach of the hearing of any of his domestics. Henry marks the asymmetry that made her compliance possible: Tamar is willing to humour him, her chaste and virtuous soul having not the least thought of that which his polluted breast is full of, and therefore she makes no scruple of being alone with him there. Keil and Delitzsch record the request that completed the manoeuvre, that she bring the food into the chamber so that he might eat it from her hand, and note that she took the cakes she had made and brought them in to Amnon her brother.
11:
The pretence ends the moment she is within reach. Gill notes how far she had been drawn in — not only into the chamber but to the side of the bed or couch where Amnon had placed himself, in a position proper to answer his purpose. Keil and Delitzsch record the seizure and the words together: he took hold of her and told her to lie with him, addressing her as his sister. Henry marks the collapse of the whole device: the mask is thrown off and the meat thrown by, and the wretch who calls her sister in the same breath courts her to such wickedness — which Henry counts a base affront to her virtue.

Her first argument is drawn from the law of her nation. Gill observes that the opening words carried their own sufficient reason, since he was her brother and she his sister, and such an indignity ought not to be offered her. Ellicott describes her as reasoning her way toward escape, and identifies the source she reaches for: she speaks of the sinfulness in Israel of what was permitted among the surrounding heathen, quoting the very words of Genesis 34:7, as if by the traditions of their nation to recall the king's son to a sense of right. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the allusion, noting that the term for folly is first used there to denote a want of chastity, and that such a sin was altogether out of keeping with the calling and holiness of Israel (Leviticus 20:8). Wesley presses the fraternal duty the other way: nature both teaches a brother to abhor such thoughts and obliges him to defend her from such a mischief at his utmost hazard, were another to attempt it — and if he ought to abhor the thing even were she willing, to add violence is abominable.

Her second argument turns to what the act would cost them both. Gill expounds her shame as a loss of reputation beyond repair: in the most private and retired place she would still blush at the thought of the crime, she would be still less able to lift up her face in any public company, and she could never expect to be admitted into the matrimonial state, her character ruined. Wesley compresses it to the impossibility of either enduring or avoiding the shame, and adds that Amnon would become contemptible to all the people, whereas at present he is heir apparent to the crown. Ellicott puts the same consequence in moral terms, that such an act would mark him as one who had cast off the fear of God and the restraints of decency.

Her last suggestion is read three ways. Clarke takes it at face value, that she supposed her father would give her to Amnon as wife, and calls this a strong mark of indelicacy in those simple but barbarous times — excusable perhaps under the patriarchal age but not now; though he allows she may have said it only to divert him, so that she might get out of his hands. Ellicott rules out the literal reading on legal grounds, since the marriage of half-brother and sister was strictly forbidden (Leviticus 18:9; Leviticus 18:11; Leviticus 20:17), and holds that she made any and every suggestion to gain time and escape the pressing danger, while Amnon knew the Law too well to hope for a legitimate marriage and therefore persisted in his violence. Wesley offers a third account, that she thought her royal father might dispense with the provision on so extraordinary an occasion to save his first-born son's life. None of it reached him: Gill explains that his lust was so enraged that he could attend to no argument however forcible, and Keil and Delitzsch state the outcome without mitigation — being stronger than she, he overpowered her and forced her.
15:
The reversal is immediate, and whether it can be accounted for is itself disputed. Keil and Delitzsch treat it as intelligible: no sooner was the animal passion gratified than his love for the humbled sister turned into a hatred greater than the love had been, and they hold the change fully explicable psychologically and still frequently exemplified in actual life — a striking proof, to them, that lust is not love but simply the gratification of the animal passions. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by way of a maxim, that human nature hates one whom it has injured, and infers that Amnon was governed by mere animal passion rather than love. Clarke refuses the whole attempt, calling the conduct not only brutal but inexplicable: conjectures about the cause are easy to form, but no certainty can be arrived at.

Those who do venture a cause offer three. Gill looks to conscience — having gratified his lust it stung him, so that he could not bear the sight of the one who had been its instrument; and he adds that her sharp words, representing him as one of the fools in Israel, and perhaps sharper ones after the act, may have filled him with hatred. Henry locates it in her refusal to share the guilt: she would not consent, but resisted to the last and reasoned against it, and so threw all the blame upon him. Had he hated the sin and loathed himself for it, Henry says, there might have been hope he was penitent, since godly sorrow worketh indignation (2 Corinthians 7:11); but to hate the person he had abused showed a conscience terrified and a heart not at all humbled. Wesley reads it providentially, as the just judgment of God upon Amnon and David both, so that the sin might be made public and way made for the tragedies that follow.

Her protest against being sent away rests on a clause the commentators find hard. Gill gives the plain sense, that there was no cause for such treatment as this. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew is elliptical and difficult and that various interpretations have been suggested, among which the Authorised Version expresses the sense well without being an accurate translation. Keil and Delitzsch supply the missing verb and read her as pleading that he not add to the great wrong already done her the still greater one of thrusting her away, which they regard as the only admissible explanation of the expression.

Why the expulsion should be the greater of the two wrongs is then set out. Keil and Delitzsch give the reputational logic: it would inevitably be supposed that she had been guilty of some shameful conduct herself and that the seduction had come from her, whereas she was perfectly innocent and had done nothing but what affection towards a sick brother dictated — and she could not even call for help as the law prescribed (Deuteronomy 22:27), because Amnon had sent the servants away and no assistance was to be expected from them. Wesley distinguishes the two acts by kind: the first was in itself the greater sin, but this the greater cruelty and calamity, exposing her to public infamy and turning a private offence into a public scandal, to the dishonour of God and of his people and especially of the royal family. Ellicott adds the obligation Amnon had incurred, that having wronged her he was now bound to protect and comfort her. Henry measures what the manner of it cost: had the thing been concealed her honour would have been lost to herself only, and had she been given time to compose herself she might have kept her countenance and so kept her counsel; but to dismiss her thus rudely, as if she had done some wicked thing, obliged her in her own defence to proclaim the wrong done her.
17:
The expulsion is carried out at second hand, and that detail is read as deliberate. Gill notes only that the servants called were his domestic servants, those who waited on him. Keil and Delitzsch register the contempt in the wording of the order: Amnon called the boy who attended him and told him to put out this person — the sister he had just humbled — and to bolt the door behind her, so that the whole thing had the appearance of her having made a shameful proposal to him. Ellicott draws the same inference from the demonstrative, that Amnon doubtless intended to give the impression that Tamar had behaved shamefully towards him, and judges the baseness of the insinuation to be in keeping with his brutality. Henry notes that he now disdained to touch her with his own hands.

The narrator interrupts the sequence to describe her dress, and the commentators ask why. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the remark is inserted before the obedience to the command is reported, and explain the garment as a long dress with sleeves worn as a mantle, in the manner of the virgin daughters of the king. They distinguish it from ordinary wear: it was not an under-garment but was worn over the plain tunic, taking the place of the usual sleeveless robe. Clarke and Ellicott both connect the word with Joseph, Ellicott noting that it occurs only here and in that narrative (Genesis 37:3) and is supposed to mean a tunic with long sleeves, in distinction from the short-sleeved kind commonly worn. Wesley describes it simply as embroidered work.

Gill canvasses the possibilities at greater length and declines to settle them. Whether the garment was interwoven with threads of various colours, or embroidered with figures of flowers and animals and wrought with the needle, or painted with different colours, or made up of pieces of various colours, he holds not certain; and he reports Braunius for the view that it was none of these, and neither was Joseph's coat, but a garment with sleeves reaching to the ankles and fringed at the borders. He adds a consideration that cuts against the plain reading, that in other nations — Athens among them — garments of flowers and various colours were worn by harlots and not by virgins.

The point of the description emerges in what is done in spite of it. Ellicott states it directly: the fact is mentioned to show that Tamar must have been recognised as a royal virgin by Amnon's servant as well as by everyone else. Keil and Delitzsch draw the conclusion out, that notwithstanding a dress by which a king's daughter could at once be recognised, the servant treated her like a common woman and turned her out of the house. Gill had already noticed the effect the garment would have in the street, that it made her the more observable and so her shame the more manifest — the same robe that marked her rank advertising her disgrace.
19:
Every element of her mourning is read as a signal, though not always the same signal. Gill takes the ashes simply as a token of sorrow and distress. Wesley reads the display forensically: the ashes signified grief for some calamity that had befallen her, which concurring circumstances easily discovered; the hand upon the head was a token of grief and shame, as if she were unable and ashamed to show her face; and the crying was to manifest her abhorrency of the fact, and that it was not done by her consent. Keil and Delitzsch agree about the torn dress, which they take as a sign of grief and pain at the disgrace inflicted on her, but read the hand on the head differently — as a sign that a grievous trouble had come upon her, the hand of God resting as it were upon her (Jeremiah 2:37). Both they and Ellicott render the last clause literally — she went going and cried, meaning she cried aloud as she went.

Ellicott adds a purpose beyond expression, holding that Tamar put on every external mark of the deep grief within, and that this was not only fitting in itself but a proper means to obtain justice for her wrongs. Henry reads the same acts as self-abasement rather than appeal: she tore her fine clothes in token of grief and put ashes on her head to deform herself, loathing her own beauty and ornaments because they had occasioned Amnon's unlawful love — and Henry's summary of her condition is that she went on crying for another's sin. He records what the Jewish doctors say followed: upon this occasion a law was made that a young man and a young woman should never be alone together, since if the king's daughter could be so used, what would become of the children of private men.

Absalom's question is examined for how much it concedes. Keil and Delitzsch treat it as a euphemism for what had taken place (Genesis 39:10), which Absalom immediately conjectures; Ellicott notes that the name in the Hebrew here carries a clerical error, and that Absalom at once sees how the case stands, comforts his sister, and takes her to his own house. Henry draws a harder inference from the fact that the question needed only to be asked: it would seem Amnon was notorious for such practices, so that it was dangerous for a modest woman to be with him — something Absalom might well have known while Tamar remained wholly ignorant of it.

The counsel of silence is read by all as cover for revenge. Keil and Delitzsch say Absalom quieted her because he was determined on vengeance but wished to conceal the plan for the time. Ellicott makes the silence itself necessary to a purpose of revenge already formed, and Henry has him bid her pass by the injury for the present, designing to avenge it himself. Wesley unpacks the argument Absalom actually used, and it is an accumulation of reasons for bearing it: he is thy brother, so the injury must be forgiven and forgotten; disgracing him would be a blot to us all; thou wilt not get right from David against him, since he is as near and dear to David as thou art; thy dishonour is the less because thou wast abused by a king's son and not by any mean person; and so this evil must be borne because it cannot be revenged — which Wesley takes to be precisely how Absalom covered his design. On the final word there is a flat contradiction. Wesley glosses her desolation as giving herself up to solitude through shame and dejection of mind, where Keil and Delitzsch insist the term cannot be proved to mean single or solitary, and render it as one laid waste, the joy of her life hopelessly destroyed.
21:
Henry opens the second half of the chapter with an image from Solomon, that what is said of the beginning of strife holds for the beginning of all sin: it is as the letting forth of water, and when once the flood-gates are plucked up an inundation follows, one mischief begetting another so that it is hard to say what shall be in the end. Gill specifies what David had heard — the ravishing of Tamar, her brother's turning her out of doors in that inhuman manner, and her distress upon it. Henry grants the anger its grounds, and they are several: that his own son should do such a wicked thing and draw the king himself in as accessory to it; that it was a reproach to David for not giving Amnon a better education, a blot upon his family, the ruin of his daughter, a bad example to his kingdom, and a wrong to his son's soul.

What the verse does not say is supplied from the Greek, and its standing is weighed. Clarke records that the Septuagint adds a clause to the effect that David would not grieve the soul of Amnon his son because he loved him, since he was his first-born, and notes that the same addition is found in the Vulgate and in Josephus — so that it is possible this once formed part of the Hebrew text. Keil and Delitzsch think the clause probably gives the true reason why David let such a crime go unpunished, when the law enjoined that incest be punished with death (Leviticus 20:17); but they refuse to build on it, holding it nothing but a subjective conjecture of the translators, which does not warrant altering the text. Ellicott accepts it as doubtless in part the reason of what he calls David's guilty leniency.

Two causes for that leniency are offered, and they are weighted differently. Keil and Delitzsch allow that David's being contented with mere anger is probably to be accounted for partly by his own consciousness of guilt, having himself been guilty of adultery, but hold that it arose chiefly from his indulgent affection towards his sons and his consequent want of discipline. Ellicott puts the remembrance of his own sin forward as what tended to withhold his hand from the administration of justice. Wesley leaves the two side by side without choosing, saying that David did not punish Amnon, at least not so severely as he should, either from the consciousness of his own guilt in the like kind or from that foolish indulgence which he often showed his children.

Henry presses the question the narrative invites. Was it enough for David to be angry? He ought to have punished his son and put him to open shame, having power to do it both as a father and as a king; and in failing to, he fell into Eli's error, whose sons made themselves vile and he frowned not on them. Henry then names the real obstacle: a man cannot bear the shame those must submit to who correct in others what they are conscious of in themselves — so that if Amnon was dear to him, punishing Amnon would have been that much the greater punishment to David for his own uncleanness. His anger therefore had to serve instead of his justice, and Henry's conclusion is that this is what hardens sinners (Ecclesiastes 8:11). Ellicott reads the failure forward, finding in David's criminal weakness towards his children the source of much trouble from this time to the end of his life.
22:
The silence recorded here is read two ways, and the readings are incompatible. Keil and Delitzsch take the idiom strictly: Absalom did not speak to Amnon from good to evil, meaning not a single word either way (Genesis 24:50), and they give the reason the verse gives, that he hated him for having humbled his sister. Gill reads it as restricted to the subject rather than to speech altogether. Absalom said nothing at all to him about the rape of his sister — but not because he was sulky and would not converse with him, for then Amnon would have mistrusted that he was meditating revenge and would have been upon his guard. On the contrary, Gill has him talking freely and in appearance friendly upon other things, the better to conceal both his hatred and his design. Wesley takes the same view and states the risk that made it necessary: had Absalom wholly forborne all discourse with him, it would have raised jealousies in Amnon and in David.

Wesley adds what the silence passed over. Absalom neither debated the matter with Amnon nor threatened him for it, but seemed willing to let it go by with brotherly kindness. Henry treats the appearance of civility as the aggravation rather than the strategy, and distinguishes three things that make malice worse. The first is concealment: had Absalom reasoned the matter with his brother he might have convinced him of his sin and brought him to repentance, whereas saying nothing left Amnon's heart hardened and his own the more embittered — which is why rebuking a neighbour is set against hating him in the heart (Leviticus 19:17). Let passion have vent, Henry observes, and it will spend itself.

The second and third aggravations follow from the first. Malice gilded over with a show of friendship is the worse for it, Absalom's words being smoother than butter while war was in his heart (Proverbs 26:26); and malice harboured long is worse again, since two full years were spent nursing this root of bitterness. Henry allows that at first Absalom may not have intended to kill his brother — had he, he might have found as fair an opportunity early as the one he took at last — and may have waited only for an occasion to disgrace him or do him some lesser mischief, his hatred ripening in time into a design on his life. The measure Henry applies is the warning against letting the sun go down upon wrath (Ephesians 4:26): if one sunset gives such place to the devil, he asks what the sunsets of two full years would do.
23:
The interval of two full years is read as a tactic. Gill explains what the delay bought: Absalom let the matter alone so long that the king, Amnon and the whole family might think it quite worn out of his mind and entirely forgotten, and so might the more safely confide in him. Ellicott makes the same point and adds a second motive, that Absalom no doubt chose also to give his father full opportunity to punish Amnon's iniquity if he would; and that by this long quiet waiting he so far disarmed suspicion as to be able to carry out his purpose. Wesley counts the interval twice over — as an aggravation of a malice so implacable, and as an act of policy, so that both Amnon and David might the more securely comply with his wishes.

The occasion he chose was an ordinary one, which is part of its usefulness. Clarke notes that sheep-shearing was a time when feasts were made, to which the neighbours and relatives of the family were invited; Ellicott says the same, that sheepshearing always was and still is a time of feasting (1 Samuel 25:2). Keil and Delitzsch add that the festival was celebrated as a joyous one and that Absalom must therefore have held property at the place. On where that was, both are candid: Keil and Delitzsch cannot determine the situation precisely, taking the qualifying clause to point to somewhere on the border of the territory of Ephraim, while Ellicott calls the location quite unknown and judges only that the estate was probably not many miles from Jerusalem.

The invitation is addressed to the king first, and that order is read as deliberate. Gill notes that Absalom came to Jerusalem to invite him in person. Keil and Delitzsch report David's refusal and its stated reason, that he declined so as not to be burdensome to Absalom, and that when pressed he still would not go but blessed him — which they gloss as wishing him a pleasant and successful feast. Ellicott argues that the whole exchange worked to Absalom's advantage: he could hardly have expected the king to accept, but by pressing him he effectively disguised his real purpose and secured David's blessing into the bargain. Henry notices the practical care behind the refusal, that David would not put his son to the expense of entertaining the court, and reads it as a father giving a grown child a competency to live on and then taking care that he does not live above it.
25:
David's refusal is partial rather than flat, and Gill reads the reservation closely. The king did not object to the invitation entirely, being willing that some of the family should go but not all; and Gill thinks it probable that he particularly excepted himself and his eldest son, the heir to his crown. On that reading the next request is aimed exactly at the one exception David had made.

Absalom's second request is framed as a substitution. Keil and Delitzsch render it as a direct alternative — if the king will not go himself, may Amnon go instead — and record that David would not at first give his consent. Ellicott and Wesley both explain why Amnon in particular could be asked for plausibly: as eldest son and heir-apparent he was the natural person to represent his father at the feast. Clarke adds that Absalom could urge it with the more plausibility because he had disguised his resentment so well beforehand that he was not suspected. Wesley supplies the pretences available to him, that since the king would not come, the son next to him might honour the occasion with his company, and that his coming would be a public token of friendship between the brothers notwithstanding the former cause of difference.

Why David gave way is answered three ways. Keil and Delitzsch hold that whether his hesitation came from suspicion cannot be determined with certainty, since he eventually yielded and let Amnon and all the other king's sons go; and they argue that the lapse of time without any sign of a wish for revenge might well have made David feel quite sure he had nothing more to fear. Against that they set a cultural judgment, that this long postponement of revenge for the sake of carrying it out the more certainly is quite in the spirit of the East. Ellicott makes David's consent a matter of social impossibility rather than of conviction: he hesitated, but could not well refuse without acknowledging a suspicion he was unwilling to express, and so finally consented. Wesley reads the request as forced on Absalom, since the king plainly meant to keep his eldest son at home, and Absalom would never have mentioned Amnon by name had he not been compelled to.
27:
That the pressing worked at all is treated as the problem of the passage. Gill puts it as a reasonable expectation defeated: one would think the pressing would have increased David's suspicion if he had any, or raised it in him if he had none. His explanation is providential — David's mind was blinded, so that Amnon's incest might be punished and the threatening against David and his house be fulfilled on account of the affair of Uriah and Bathsheba. Wesley reaches for the same account in nearly the same terms, calling it strange that so urgent a desire for Amnon's company raised no suspicion in so wise a king, and concluding that God suffered him to be blinded in order to execute his judgments upon David and bring upon Amnon the just punishment of his lewdness.

What the narrative leaves out at this point is itself noticed. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the arrangement of the meal is passed over as quite subordinate to the main purpose of the narrative, and both they and Ellicott identify the clause the Septuagint adds at the end of the verse — that Absalom made a feast like the feast of a king — as nothing more than an explanatory gloss, which Keil and Delitzsch judge to have been formed on the pattern of an earlier sheep-shearing feast (1 Samuel 25:36). Henry does supply the detail, holding the entertainment to have been very plentiful because Absalom meant them all to be merry with wine, or at least counted on Amnon being so, knowing him apt to drink to excess.

The instructions are examined for their timing and their wording. Gill notes that the servants were commanded before the host and his guests sat down. Keil and Delitzsch set out the two conditions Absalom named, that Amnon's heart should first become merry with wine and that Absalom himself should give the word. Wesley reads the drunkenness as chosen for its advantages — Amnon would then least suspect and be least able to prevent the evil. Henry presses the point further and makes it the first aggravation: Amnon was to be struck when least apprehensive of danger, least able to resist, and also least fit to go out of the world, as though the malice aimed at both soul and body in not giving him time to ask for mercy.

The closing question in the order is read as an assumption of liability. Keil and Delitzsch take the words to imply that Absalom would take the responsibility upon himself. Wesley expands what the servants were being offered: Absalom is the king's son and, once Amnon is gone, his heir, and so can easily obtain their pardon and reward them liberally. Henry treats the same clause as an open defiance of the divine law, since the command against killing is express, and yet Absalom issues the warrant on his own authority alone. From this he draws a rule that runs in both directions — those servants are ill taught who obey their masters in contradiction to God, and those are wicked masters who have taught them so, since masters must always command their servants as men who know they have themselves a Master in heaven.
29:
The execution is reported in a single clause, and the obedience behind it is what the witnesses examine. Gill records only that they smote him and killed him when Absalom gave the word. Ellicott explains the compliance as unremarkable in itself, since it was quite customary for the servants of a prince to obey his orders without question, leaving the entire responsibility to rest with him. Henry refuses to let that settle it, holding that servants who obey a master in contradiction to God are ill taught, and that those who will damn their souls to please their masters trust in big words that cannot secure them from God's wrath.

A second motive is suspected behind the first. Ellicott observes that if Chileab was already dead, as seems probable, Absalom stood next in the succession after Amnon; and whatever his own intention may have been, his retainers may have looked upon the killing as a preparatory step towards the throne. Henry states the suspicion about Absalom directly, that there is reason to think he did this not only to revenge his sister's quarrel but to make way for himself to the throne, which he was ambitious of and would stand fair for once the eldest son was taken off — and he accounts for the servants' readiness by their expectation that a master now next heir to the crown would save them from harm.

Henry adds an aggravation drawn from who was watching. The thing was done in the presence of all the king's sons, who were themselves chief rulers, so that it was an affront to the public justice they administered and to the king their father whom they represented, and a contempt of the sword that should have been a terror to evildoers — whereas here the evil deed was a terror to those who bore it. Of the flight that followed, Henry notes only that they came home in terror, not knowing how far their brother's bloody design might extend, and his comment is on what sin does in families.

The detail of the mules draws a note on custom. Ellicott points out that although David had reserved a number of horses from the spoil of his Syrian victories (2 Samuel 8:4), the mule was still the mount of persons of distinction (2 Samuel 18:9; 1 Kings 1:33), and that while the breeding of mules was forbidden in the Law (Leviticus 19:19) they were brought in by commerce (1 Kings 10:25). Ellicott also accounts for the princes' inaction, the blow being too sudden and unexpected to allow of interference. Wesley closes on the threat hanging over the house: the promised sword is now drawn in David's family and will not depart from it, the eldest son falling by it through his own wickedness and his father, by his connivance, accessory to it.
30:
The first report to reach Jerusalem is false, and the witnesses are interested in why false reports take that shape. Gill places the moment precisely, while the king's sons were still on the road homewards and before they reached the city. Clarke makes it an instance of a general law, that fame never lessens but always magnifies a fact, and that report, contrary to the nature of all other things, gains strength by going — for which he quotes Virgil's personification of Fame as the swift plague that every moment grows and gains new vigour as she goes. Henry states the same observation more plainly, that it is common for fame to make bad worse, and that the first news of such a thing represents it as more dreadful than it afterwards proves. His counsel follows from it: not to be afraid of evil tidings while they want confirmation, but when we hear the worst to hope at least for better.

Ellicott turns the exaggeration into an argument about the book itself, holding that a story of this kind, so true to life, indicates contemporaneous authorship. Henry observes that the falsehood cost David nothing less than the truth would have, since the news gave him as much affliction for the present as if it had been true — he tore his garments and lay on the earth while as yet it was only a flying story. Henry's comment is on the king's temperament rather than his grief: it was well that David had grace, for he had need enough of it, having strong passions.

The mourning itself is described closely. Gill reads the torn garments as a token of extreme grief and sorrow, and compares Jacob when he was shown the coat of Joseph and supposed him slain, as David supposed of all his sons. Ellicott corrects the rendering, preferring rent his clothes, the words being the same as in the last clause of the verse. Keil and Delitzsch add the posture and the silence around it: the king rent his clothes in horror at such a deed and sat down upon the ground, while all his courtiers stood by with their clothes rent as well — and they follow Bttcher in taking the verb to mean standing perfectly motionless, a sense it frequently carries (Numbers 22:23; Exodus 5:20).
32:
The man who corrects the report is the man who began the trouble, and no witness lets that pass. Gill identifies Jonadab as the same who advised Amnon to feign sickness so that Tamar might be sent to him. Keil and Delitzsch name him as the person who had helped Amnon commit his crime. Ellicott calls him the same subtle counsellor who had led Amnon into his sin, and credits him with at once divining how the case really stood and reassuring the king. Clarke draws the moral conclusion the others leave implicit, that this was a very bad man, who here speaks coolly of a most bloody tragedy which he had himself contrived. Henry's description is of the manner rather than the man, calling these the sly suggestions by which the mistake was put right.

What Jonadab knew, and how he knew it, turns on a difficult phrase. Ellicott renders it literally — upon Absalom's mouth it hath been set — notes that it has given rise to much variety of interpretation, and judges that the Authorised Version expresses the sense accurately. Keil and Delitzsch offer two possible meanings, either that the murder might be seen by Absalom's own mouth or that it might be gathered from what he had said, and gloss the construction as a thing laid down, that is, determined (Exodus 21:13). On either reading Jonadab's certainty rests on Absalom's own talk, which makes the design one that had been audible to anyone listening since the day Tamar was forced.

The correction is pressed twice, and the repetition is noted. Gill glosses the plea as asking the king neither to suppose the thing nor to be troubled for it. Keil and Delitzsch explain the grammar of the denial, that the particle is used in the sense of no, but, the negation being implied in the thought that the king should not take to heart what they are saying about all his sons. Henry treats Jonadab's intervention as only the first of two ways in which the mistake was rectified, since he could tell David both that Amnon alone was dead and that the thing had been done by Absalom's appointment, determined from the day Amnon forced his sister.

Keil and Delitzsch then address an apparent disorder in the narrative. The statement that Absalom fled follows on from the account of the murder, the intervening verses being a parenthesis in which the writer describes the impression made upon the king and his court by the report. They explain the seemingly unsuitable placing from the sequence of events, the flight of Absalom having preceded the arrival of the rest of the sons at the palace; and they reject Bttcher's proposal to remove the statement from the text on account of its position, since the account of Absalom's flight cannot possibly be left out, being referred to again later.
34:
Absalom's flight is reported out of sequence, and Ellicott explains why it has to be. The statement connects backwards to the murder and forwards to the later account of where he went, several things having happened at once: when the king's sons fled towards the palace, Absalom took advantage of the confusion and escaped another way. The reason for mentioning it just here, Ellicott argues, is that otherwise he would seem to be included among the king's sons of the two following verses — so the notice is placed where it is to keep him out of a group he was no longer part of.

Gill reads the flight as an admission of what the law required. The man who had promised his servants protection could not protect himself, and the servants no doubt fled with him; for he knew that what he had done was death by law, that there was no city of refuge available for such a murder as this, and that he had no reason to hope the king would let so foul a crime pass unpunished. On Gill's account the flight is therefore not panic but calculation, and it concedes the case against him.

The watchman's report is described from his own vantage. The people are seen coming by the way of the hill side behind him, which Ellicott glosses as meaning from the west — the Oriental being always supposed to face the east when speaking of the points of the compass. Gill notes what closer approach settled, that as they came nearer it was plainly discovered that these were the king's sons, seen on the side of the hill.

Jonadab uses the sighting to claim vindication. Keil and Delitzsch record that he had hardly finished speaking when the king's sons arrived; and the form of his announcement is that the thing has turned out as he said it would. Gill's gloss keeps to the identification itself, that what the watchman saw at a distance resolved into the returning princes, which is the first independent confirmation the king receives that the report he had been given was false.
36:
The confirmation arrives on the heels of the correction. Gill marks the timing exactly, that it happened as soon as the words were out of Jonadab's mouth. Keil and Delitzsch describe what followed: the king's sons came and wept aloud as they related what had occurred, whereupon the king and all his retainers broke out in loud weeping. The grief is therefore not the grief of the false report but a second grief, informed this time, and it is shared by the whole court.

The next verse doubles back, and the witnesses treat the repetition as a feature of the writing. Gill notes simply that Absalom's flight has been related before and is repeated here for the sake of what follows. Keil and Delitzsch take the clause as a circumstantial one inserted as a parenthesis, in order to define the expression the king's sons more particularly — that is, to make clear that Absalom was not among those who returned. They account for the repetition itself by the general diffuseness of the Hebrew style, and note that to the remark about David's mourning is attached the further information that Absalom remained in Geshur three years.

Where he fled is explained by the family connection. Keil and Delitzsch identify Talmai king of Geshur as the father of Maacah, Absalom's mother (2 Samuel 3:3), and observe that the Septuagint thought it necessary to indicate this expressly. Clarke draws out the legal position that made such a refuge necessary: having committed wilful murder, Absalom could not avail himself of a city of refuge, and was therefore obliged to leave the land of Israel altogether and take shelter with his grandfather on his mother's side. Wesley adds the two things Absalom stood to gain there, present protection and sustenance from Talmai, and the hope that by his grandfather's mediation he might obtain his father's pardon.

Who David mourned for is settled by grammar and by sense. Both Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch observe that David is not named in the latter clause and must be supplied from the preceding verse, which follows naturally once the notice about Absalom is read as a parenthesis. Ellicott is explicit about the object of the grief, that Amnon is certainly the son meant, for whom David continually mourned until the lapse of time gradually assuaged it. Keil and Delitzsch put the mourning for Amnon at the whole of David's life, which sets the three years of Absalom's absence inside a sorrow that outlasted them.
38:
The flight is mentioned for the third time, and Ellicott makes the repetition purposeful. After the custom of Scripture narrative each mention introduces some additional fact: the first states the bare flight, the second adds that he went to his grandfather, and this one that he remained with him three years. Gill reports a different explanation from Abarbinel, which turns on a change in Absalom's own conduct. At first he stood openly in the court of his grandfather's palace and travelled with him wherever he went; but learning how bitterly his father mourned for Amnon, he grew afraid David would send to lay hold of him, and so went abroad with the king of Geshur no more but abode there always — Geshur being, as Gill notes, a fortified city.

The last verse is the hardest in the chapter, and the division over it is complete. Gill records that the opening words are supplied, the Targum paraphrasing in this way because the verb rendered longed is feminine — though he allows the feminine form may instead mark the effeminacy of David's disposition and carriage on this occasion. He preserves two Jewish alternatives: Aben Ezra would supply the word wife, so that Absalom's mother petitioned the king to fetch her son and by her importunity stirred up a longing in David after him; while Abarbinel reports another who held that throughout the three years David sought vengeance continually, until a woman — his mother, or Tamar, or his daughter — was importunate with him and restrained both the king and his servants from going forth.

Ellicott sets out the received reading and then dismantles it. The English sense, which is also that of the Chaldee and the Jewish commentators, is that David's grief for Amnon having abated he longed after Absalom and pined for his return; against which Ellicott urges three things — that there is no ground for supplying the ellipsis in that way, that the verb is a common one which nowhere else bears the sense given it, and that the picture is contrary to fact, since David could easily have recalled Absalom had he wished, yet when Absalom was actually brought back through Joab's stratagem the king refused to see him (2 Samuel 14:24) and only after two years more admitted him reluctantly to his presence (2 Samuel 14:28). The better interpretation, he holds, takes the verb impersonally and yields the opposite sense: David desisted from going forth against Absalom. He ought to have arrested and punished him for a murder that was at once fratricide and high treason, being the assassination of the heir-apparent; but the flight to Geshur made that difficult, and as time passed he gave the thought up.

Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by the grammar, rendering the clause as something that held the king back from going out to Absalom, taking the feminine verb as an impersonal with its subject left indefinite, and noting that going out to a man carries a hostile sense (Deuteronomy 28:7) — that is, going out to punish him. Clarke and Wesley read the verse the other way and judge David by it. Clarke finds a very strong paternal affection for a young man who had little to commend him but the beauty of his person, notes that Joab marked the disposition and worked on it to procure the return, and concludes it would have been well for all parties had Absalom ended his days at Geshur, since his return brought increasing wretchedness to his unfortunate father. Wesley is blunter, asking how David is to be excused for honouring his sons above God: at first he could not find in his heart to do justice to the ravisher of his sister, and now he can almost find in his heart to receive into favour the murderer of his brother.
